drills.q: What machine does asymptotic notation assume?
options: One where memory is flat and every access costs the same
One with a two level cache and a prefetcher
Whichever machine the algorithm will run on
One with a single core and no pipeline
drills.why: It was close enough to true when the model was written down, and it has not been true for about thirty years.

drills.q: Two structures with the same complexity, the same allocation and the same operation count measured how far apart?
options: Twelve times at small sizes, growing past six hundred at large ones
Within a factor of two, as the notation implies
About ten times, at every size
They measured the same; the difference is folklore
drills.why: The gap is not a fixed constant. It grows with the input, because it tracks which level of the hierarchy the structure has fallen out of.

drills.q: In that measurement, what was the only variable?
options: The order the pointers linked the same nodes in
Whether the nodes were heap allocated or not
The size of each node
Whether the compiler could vectorise the loop
drills.why: Both lists used the same pool with identical allocation, which removes "linked lists allocate badly" as an explanation and leaves the visiting order.

drills.q: A linked list walked in memory order costs how much more than an array?
options: A few times, and that ratio does not grow with the input
A hundred times, like the shuffled case
Nothing measurable
It grows in the same way the shuffled case does
drills.why: The middle column of the table is the explanation. The cost is not that linked lists are slow.

drills.q: Why is a sequential walk cheap?
options: The addresses advance by a fixed stride, so the hardware fetches the next line before it is asked for
The compiler unrolls it
It touches fewer elements
Sequential loads bypass the cache entirely
drills.why: A fixed stride is trivially predictable, which is the whole of what a prefetcher needs.

drills.q: Why can a pointer chase not overlap its misses?
options: The address of the next load is the result of the current one, so it cannot be issued early
The cache refuses more than one outstanding miss
The nodes are too large to fit in a line fill buffer
The compiler serialises pointer arithmetic
drills.why: It is a dependent chain by construction, which is the difference between paying for a dozen misses at once and paying for each one alone.

drills.q: What is the difference between bandwidth bound and latency bound here?
options: Whether many misses are in flight at once, sharing the cost, or one at a time paying the full round trip
Whether the data is read or written
Whether the working set exceeds the last level cache
Whether the access pattern is aligned
drills.why: A dozen outstanding line fills is the machine's capacity, and a dependent chain cannot use any of them.

drills.q: Roughly what does a main memory access cost, relative to a first level hit?
options: About a hundred times
About five times
About ten times
About a thousand times
drills.why: The shape to memorise is one, five, twenty, a hundred, for the first level, the second, the third and main memory.

drills.q: Roughly what does a same datacentre network round trip cost, relative to a first level hit?
options: About five hundred thousand times
About a thousand times
About fifty thousand times
About five million times
drills.why: Each big gap in that ladder is a design boundary. The one before it, at about fifty thousand, is storage, and it is why trees with thousands of children per node exist.

drills.q: How do you read a machine's cache sizes out of a timing curve?
options: Chase a random cycle of pointers over growing working sets and look for the knees
Read them from the operating system, which is the only reliable way
Time a sequential scan and divide by the line size
Measure the bandwidth at each size and find where it halves
drills.why: A random cycle defeats both the prefetcher and any overlap between misses, which exposes the true load to use latency. The knees land exactly on the reported sizes.

options: Latency; main memory has sat between seventy and a hundred nanoseconds for over fifteen years while bandwidth went up twentyfold
Bandwidth, which has been flat since clock speeds stopped rising
Both, at the same rate
Neither; both continue to improve with process nodes
drills.why: That is why almost every technique in this part is a way of trading latency for bandwidth.

drills.q: Why was the measured ratio higher than the latency arithmetic predicted?
options: A second dependent load, and a working set with far more pages than the translation cache holds
The measurement included allocation time
The compiler failed to optimise the array case
Thermal throttling during the longer run
drills.why: A hundred and twenty eight megabytes at sixteen kilobyte pages is eight thousand pages, so most accesses pay for a page walk too. It is the reason large pages exist as a tuning option.

drills.q: What is asymptotic notation still the right tool for?
options: Deciding whether an approach can work at all as the input grows without bound
Choosing between two algorithms with the same growth
Predicting the running time on a particular machine
Comparing two data structures with the same operation counts
drills.why: No amount of constant factor tuning rescues a quadratic algorithm on a large input, and the notation tells you that before you write anything.

drills.q: When is a linked list the right structure?
options: When you need to splice a sublist in constant time, or a reference that stays valid while the container changes
When insertions are more common than traversals
When the element count is not known in advance
When elements are large and expensive to move
drills.why: It is never right because inserting is cheap. Insertion is constant time given the node, and finding the node is the worst kind of linear there is.

drills.q: Why does an array beat a list at inserting into a sorted sequence, despite moving half its elements?
options: Moving a block of memory runs at tens of gigabytes a second, and the list's traversal is a chain of full latency misses
The array insert is amortised constant time
Compilers vectorise the shifting loop
The comparison assumes the list is unsorted
drills.why: The array does strictly more work by the operation count and still wins for essentially every size, which is the whole argument of the unit in one example.
